member.name: M:GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.StartStreaming(GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.Format,System.Int32)
member.summary: Starts streaming the chosen format. Allocates the device-side double buffer.
member.param: One of the entries from .

Requested frame rate. Default is 15 — the slowest rate that virtually every UVC camera supports, so it's the broadest-compatibility starting point. Pass 0 to use the camera's own default rate (typically 30 fps) from the frame descriptor. Any other value asks the camera for that rate; the camera rounds to its nearest supported value (visible in the PROBE GET_CUR exchange).
Use this to throttle a camera that produces faster than your application can consume: cheap UVC cameras often have an internal FIFO and produce at their max rate regardless. If you can render at 10 fps but the camera produces at 30, 20 fps of frames pile up in its FIFO per second, manifesting as a several-second "playback delayed behind reality" lag. Setting to match your app's processing rate keeps producer and consumer aligned and eliminates the lag. When the camera refuses to go below its minimum supported rate, use periodically to flush its internal FIFO instead.

member.name: M:GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.Resync(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Flushes any frames the camera has queued in its internal sensor->encoder FIFO.
member.param:
false (default) — hard flush via streaming alt-setting toggle. Definitive on every UVC camera but ~500-1000 ms blackout because the camera reboots its sensor pipeline.
true — soft flush, replays the previously negotiated SET_CUR (Commit) only. ~20 ms blackout. Camera-dependent: some cameras flush their FIFO on commit-during-streaming, others ignore it and the call is effectively a no-op. Try once on your specific camera and fall back to false if the lag doesn't drop.
member.remarks: Some UVC cameras capture internally faster than they can ship over USB and accumulate the difference in an internal FIFO, producing a "screen lags real life" effect that grows over time. Calling Resync drops the camera's internal queue so the next frame the application receives reflects the moment of the call rather than several seconds ago. Application chooses the cadence. Throws if not currently streaming.

member.name: M:GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.GetFrame(System.Byte[])
member.summary: Copies the most recently completed frame into as raw bytes.
member.param: Destination buffer. Must be at least bytes (which is the upper bound; actual size returned).
member.returns: Actual number of bytes written. For YUY2 always Width*Height*2. For MJPEG, varies per frame.
member.remarks:
Returned bytes are the camera's raw stream:
For YUY2 ( == false): YUYV-packed pixels (Y1 U Y2 V tuples). Use to convert.
For MJPEG ( == true): a complete JPEG-encoded frame. Decode with your JPEG decoder.
The driver does not pre-convert pixel formats — application controls conversion timing/threading.

member.name: M:GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.ConvertYuy2ToRgb565(System.Byte[],System.Byte[])
member.summary: Converts a YUY2 (YUYV-packed) buffer to RGB565 in place into .
member.param: Source buffer with YUY2-packed pixels (Y1 U Y2 V tuples).
Destination buffer for RGB565 pixels (2 bytes per pixel).
member.remarks: Output byte count equals input byte count (4 source bytes -> 2 RGB565 pixels = 4 dest bytes). Internally the byte count is rounded down to a multiple of 4. Uses BT.601 conversion math performed in native code.

member.name: M:GHIElectronics.TinyCLR.Devices.UsbHost.Webcam.CheckEvents(System.Object)
member.summary: Polled by BaseDevice's worker; raises FrameAvailable when a new frame lands.
member.remarks: The handler is invoked synchronously here, so a slow event handler (e.g. JPEG decode taking longer than the timer's polling interval) would otherwise let timer callbacks queue up — every cycle adds (handler_time − interval) of backlog, producing a multi-second offset between the camera's view and what's rendered. The processingFrame guard makes CheckEvents return immediately while a previous invocation is still running. The native double-buffer keeps only the most recent frame anyway, so dropping intermediates preserves real-time playback at the cost of an occasionally-skipped frame on slow handlers.
